summary: A 1975 proposal that extends the message field definitions begun in RFC 561, in an effort to set syntactic and semantic standards for ARPANET messages. It sits in the line of work that led to RFC 733 and RFC 822.

eli5.summary: Early network mail needed labels like To and From. This note adds more labels so messages describe themselves better.

subtitle: A 1975 proposal that defines more ARPANET message header fields on top of the RFC 561 format.

tldr.problem: Sites that wanted to use message fields beyond those in RFC 561 had no common standard for their syntax and meaning.
tldr.mechanism: The document restates the basic message syntax and then defines header fields for originators, references, receivers and message type, using angle brackets for machine-readable notations.
tldr.outcome: The format is compatible with RFC 561, and not every message server is expected to process all the fields. It updates RFC 561, and the specification is deliberately very general to allow experimentation.

today: RFC 680 is a 1975 proposal that updates RFC 561. Its status is listed as Unknown, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Goal and Approach
sections.content:
RFC 680 defines message fields beyond those discussed in RFC 561. The overall message format stays compatible with RFC 561 and makes extensive use of its miscellaneous fields. The aim is to establish ARPANET standards for the syntax and semantics of the extra fields.

The authors expect that not all fields will be processed automatically by every message server. The standard is needed so sites that want to use them have something to work from. They also say it "attempts to tread the narrow line" between features for people and for machines, and that machine-readable notations are generally in angle brackets so programs can tell whether and where to look. The specification is made excessively general to allow experimentation.
sections.eli5: People wanted extra labels on their mail, so this note writes down what the labels are called and what they mean.

sections.title: Basic Message Syntax
sections.content:
Section I repeats the relevant syntax from RFC 561. A message is a header, a blank line (CRLF) and a body. The required header is a DATE: item (a date, AT, a four-digit time and a zone such as EST or GMT) followed by a SENDER: item naming a user AT a host.

Optional items include SUBJECT:, Message-ID:, the addressee items TO:, CC: and BCC:, and other keywords such as FROM, IN-REPLY-TO, REFERENCES, KEYWORD, PRECEDENCE, MESSAGE-CLASS, SPECIAL-HANDLING, AUTHENTICATION and ACCESSION-KEY. A message may have at most one MESSAGE-ID item, and the case of keywords is insignificant.
sections.eli5: A message has a top part with labels and a bottom part with the words, and the top part has a few labels that every message must have.

sections.title: Originator, Reference and Receiver Fields
sections.content:
FROM is the person who wished the message to be sent, and SENDER is the person who sends it, normally set automatically. The usage differs from RFC 561. AUTHENTICATION says which originator fields have been authenticated and by which operating systems.

MESSAGE-ID is a unique identifier in the form [Net Address]Text String, with examples [ISIB]7-DEC-74.14:23:45 and [ARC]QLOURNAL 39274a3. Uniqueness is guaranteed per net-address, not per site name. IN-REPLY-TO and REFERENCES identify earlier correspondence, with message identifiers in angle brackets, and KEYWORDS holds comma-separated phrases.

TO names the primary receivers, CC the secondary receivers and BCC the tertiary receivers. BCC should not be shown to the primary and secondary receivers, though it may be recorded for access control.
sections.eli5: FROM says who wanted the message sent and SENDER says who actually sent it. TO, CC and BCC say who gets it, and BCC is a secret copy.

sections.title: Message-Type Fields
sections.content:
PRECEDENCE describes importance and urgency. <PRIORITY> means deliver as soon as possible and <ROUTINE> means priority processing is not necessary. MESSAGE-CLASS describes the legal status of the message, with examples such as Official, Unofficial, Record, Off the Record and Junk Mail, and no automatic processing is expected.

SPECIAL-HANDLING gives instructions for the receiving end. <PRIVATE> means the reception process should not help the user circulate copies to others. Plain text may be added to both PRECEDENCE and SPECIAL-HANDLING.
sections.eli5: These labels say how urgent a message is, how official it is, and whether it should be kept private.

references.text: RFC 561, the base message format that RFC 680 extends and updates.
